newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil price gains capped by supply worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil price gains capped by supply worries.

text.p: World oil prices made limited gains on Tuesday with market players willing to buy only up to a point as worries over a supply glut persisted.
Speculators that sold the market to a new 13-month low last week were now keen to buy to cover short positions -- and not to miss out on a rally.
"We're really approaching levels where people are not prepared to sell," one dealer said. But he added: "We're not bullish yet, we need a few more days of consolidation."
London July futures for Benchmark Brent Blend crude were 34 cents higher at $18.20 a barrel by 1600 GMT.
Concerns over Middle East political tensions helped underpin oil.
The United States on Tuesday said Iran had tested a new Chinese air-launched anti-ship cruise missile in the oil rich Gulf.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen warned Tehran against any attempt at halting shipping in the region.

"The short side of the oil market was getting a little stale and started looking for excuses to rally. Iran was one of these excuses," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at brokerage Smith Barney.

Dealers also continued to fret that ongoing delays to the second six-month tranche of Iraqi exports covered by a humanitarian agreement between the United Nations and Iraq would stifle Middle East supply and buoy prices.
Iraqi envoy Nizar Hamdoon said last week no more oil would be exported until Baghdad received assurances on the distribution of food and medicine bought with the proceeds of its crude exports.

And on Tuesday Baghdad accused the United States and Britain of blocking implementation of the oil-for-food deal. The Baghdad mayor said Iraq received less than half the goods supposed to reach the country during the first six months of the pact.
"Six months of the deal have ended and six months more were added, but the United States and Britain are obstructing implementation of the deal," he said.

While the Iraqi saga and some buying to cover futures positions were buoying the market, brokers said any gains were very much capped as signals from elsewhere in the world reinforced concerns of oversupply.

Figures showing a increase in the loading schedule for the North Sea in July reinforced this view. Schedules released this week by operating companies in Britain and Norway showed an increase of 190,000 barrels per day (bpd) from June to 4.49 million bpd.
And there were some market jitters ahead of the OPEC ministerial meeting in Vienna on June 25 with players worried the cartel would fail to agree on stringent adherence to production quotas.
While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia are maintaining spare capacity and quota discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria are pumping at full steam without regard for oil prices.
"I'm not convinced the market's going to stay up here. With the OPEC meeting next week, I think some people are going to get out," one broker said.
There were also signs of oversupply in the Far East with Shell Singapore initiating a plan to cut refinery crude runs.
Shell said the cut in June refinery output to 57,000 tonnes per day from 59,000 was "as a response to market conditions."
